pack.description: Academic collocations: word partnerships that make written and spoken arguments sound natural.
pack.selection_note: Internal high-yield selection of word combinations that recur in academic writing and discussion; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: to be one of the things that cause or influence a result
entries.example_academic: Diet plays a role in the development of the disease, but genes matter more.
entries.example_spoken: Luck played a role, but she also worked really hard.

entries.definition: to decide that something is true after thinking about the facts
entries.example_academic: It is too early to draw a conclusion from a single season of data.
entries.example_spoken: Don't draw a conclusion before you've read the whole article.

entries.definition: to carry out a careful study in order to discover new facts
entries.example_academic: The team conducted research on sleep patterns among shift workers.
entries.example_spoken: She's conducting research on bees for her thesis.

entries.definition: to make more people know about a problem or subject
entries.example_academic: The campaign raised awareness of the risks of antibiotic overuse.
entries.example_spoken: We're selling coffee to raise awareness about food waste.

entries.definition: to be something that could cause harm or danger
entries.example_academic: Rising sea levels pose a threat to coastal cities.
entries.example_spoken: Does the construction pose a threat to the old trees?

entries.definition: to produce a strong effect on someone or something
entries.example_academic: Early childhood education has an impact on earnings decades later.
entries.example_spoken: The new schedule had a big impact on my sleep.

entries.definition: to consider something when you are judging a situation or making a decision
entries.example_academic: The estimate does not take into account the cost of maintenance.
entries.example_spoken: You have to take the commute into account when you choose an apartment.

entries.definition: to recognize or point out that two things are different
entries.example_academic: The author makes a distinction between income and wealth.
entries.example_spoken: We need to make a distinction between urgent and important tasks.

entries.definition: to collect facts or numbers for a study
entries.example_academic: Researchers gathered data from more than two hundred schools.
entries.example_spoken: We're gathering data for our survey in the cafeteria.

entries.definition: to watch, listen to or think about something carefully
entries.example_academic: Earlier studies paid little attention to the role of women in the trade.
entries.example_spoken: Pay attention to the dates; they'll be on the test.

entries.definition: a large number of different things of the same general kind
entries.example_academic: The enzyme is active across a wide range of temperatures.
entries.example_spoken: The gym offers a wide range of classes.

entries.definition: to move forward in your work or toward a goal
entries.example_academic: Researchers have made progress toward a vaccine in recent years.
entries.example_spoken: I finally made progress on my essay last night.

entries.definition: to get knowledge or skill by doing something over time
entries.example_academic: Graduates gain experience through placements in local firms.
entries.example_spoken: I want to gain experience before I apply for a master's.

entries.definition: to do or have what a rule or standard demands
entries.example_academic: Buildings constructed before the reform do not meet the requirements for fire safety.
entries.example_spoken: Does this course meet the requirement for my major?

entries.definition: to cause people to think about or discuss a matter
entries.example_academic: The findings raise a question about the reliability of earlier surveys.
entries.example_spoken: That raises a question: who's going to pay for it?

entries.definition: to give facts that show something is true
entries.example_academic: The fossils provide evidence of a much warmer climate.
entries.example_spoken: Can you provide evidence that you were sick?

entries.definition: to use an opportunity or situation to get a benefit
entries.example_academic: Firms took advantage of low interest rates to expand.
entries.example_spoken: You should take advantage of the free tutoring.

entries.definition: to try hard to do something
entries.example_academic: The government made an effort to consult rural communities.
entries.example_spoken: He made an effort to arrive on time this week.

entries.definition: over a period of time that continues far into the future
entries.example_academic: In the long term, investment in education raises national income.
entries.example_spoken: In the long term, it's cheaper to buy a bike than to take the bus.

entries.definition: to talk formally to a group of people about a subject
entries.example_academic: Each student gives a presentation on a published article.
entries.example_spoken: I have to give a presentation in my seminar tomorrow.

entries.definition: to choose what to do after thinking about it
entries.example_academic: The committee will make a decision once all the reports have been received.
entries.example_spoken: I need to make a decision about housing by Friday.

entries.definition: more and more of a particular kind of person or thing
entries.example_academic: A growing number of studies link air quality to school performance.
entries.example_spoken: A growing number of students are taking classes online.

entries.definition: to accept that you are the person who must deal with something or who caused it
entries.example_academic: Local councils took responsibility for maintaining the roads.
entries.example_spoken: Someone has to take responsibility for booking the room.

entries.definition: to decide what you want to achieve
entries.example_academic: The agreement set a goal of halving emissions within twenty years.
entries.example_spoken: I set a goal of reading one article a day.

entries.definition: to finish something by the time it is due
entries.example_academic: Contractors who fail to meet a deadline pay a daily penalty.
entries.example_spoken: We met the deadline with ten minutes to spare.

entries.definition: to arrive at an opinion or decision that everyone in a group accepts
entries.example_academic: Scientists have reached a consensus on the main causes of the decline.
entries.example_spoken: We couldn't reach a consensus on the topic, so we voted.

entries.definition: to remember a fact and consider it when you decide or judge something
entries.example_academic: Readers should bear in mind that the figures are estimates.
entries.example_spoken: Bear in mind that the library closes early on Fridays.

entries.definition: to make something easier to understand by providing new information
entries.example_academic: The letters shed light on the daily life of ordinary soldiers.
entries.example_spoken: Can you shed some light on why the meeting was cancelled?

entries.definition: to find a sensible middle point between two opposite needs
entries.example_academic: Planners must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
entries.example_spoken: I'm trying to strike a balance between work and sleep.

entries.definition: opinions or interests that people share even though they disagree about other things
entries.example_academic: The two schools of thought share more common ground than their supporters admit.
entries.example_spoken: We finally found some common ground on the budget.

entries.definition: to create the basic conditions that make a later development possible
entries.example_academic: These early experiments laid the foundation for modern genetics.
entries.example_spoken: The first-year courses lay the foundation for everything that follows.

entries.definition: a large amount of information that together supports a conclusion
entries.example_academic: A substantial body of evidence links exercise to improved memory.
entries.example_spoken: There's a whole body of evidence showing that cramming doesn't work.

entries.definition: to show that two things are similar in some way
entries.example_academic: The author draws a parallel between the two revolutions.
entries.example_spoken: You could draw a parallel between learning a language and learning music.

entries.definition: to reduce or remove the difference between two groups or things
entries.example_academic: The program aims to bridge the gap between school and university.
entries.example_spoken: Summer classes helped me bridge the gap in math.

entries.definition: to make people doubt whether something is true or right
entries.example_academic: The new measurements call into question the accepted age of the site.
entries.example_spoken: That mistake calls the whole report into question.

entries.definition: in a way that harms or reduces something else
entries.example_academic: Output rose at the expense of product quality.
entries.example_spoken: He got good grades at the expense of his health.

entries.definition: after considering a particular fact or new piece of information
entries.translation_fr: compte tenu de, à la lumière de
entries.example_academic: In light of these findings, the earlier model must be revised.
entries.example_spoken: In light of the weather, we're moving the event indoors.

entries.definition: to come to understand something more deeply
entries.translation_fr: mieux comprendre, avoir un aperçu de
entries.example_academic: Interviews allowed the researchers to gain insight into the workers' motives.
entries.example_spoken: The internship helped me gain insight into how a newsroom works.

entries.definition: believed or approved by most people
entries.example_academic: It is widely accepted that early diagnosis improves outcomes.
entries.example_spoken: It's widely accepted that you learn more by teaching others.

entries.definition: a question about which people still disagree
entries.example_academic: The exact date of the migration remains a matter of debate.
entries.example_spoken: Whether attendance should count is still a matter of debate.

entries.definition: facts that are strong enough to make people believe something
entries.example_academic: The trial produced compelling evidence that the drug reduces mortality.
entries.example_spoken: There's no compelling evidence that the shortcut is faster.

entries.definition: results that affect many people or things over a long time
entries.example_academic: The decision had far-reaching consequences for trade across the region.
entries.example_spoken: Dropping that course could have far-reaching consequences for your degree.

entries.definition: a part that is more important than any other in making something happen
entries.example_academic: Merchants played a pivotal role in the spread of the new religion.
entries.example_spoken: Our team captain had a pivotal role in winning the final.

entries.definition: to use power or authority to affect what happens
entries.example_academic: Large landowners exerted influence over local courts.
entries.example_spoken: Older students exert a lot of influence on the first-years.

entries.definition: unable to be true or to exist at the same time
entries.example_academic: The two explanations are not mutually exclusive and may both apply.
entries.example_spoken: Having fun and getting good grades aren't mutually exclusive.

entries.definition: information based on personal stories rather than on careful study
entries.example_academic: The claim rests on anecdotal evidence rather than controlled trials.
entries.example_spoken: That's just anecdotal evidence; your cousin isn't a study.

entries.definition: a strong personal reason for wanting something to happen, because you will gain from it
entries.example_academic: Producers have a vested interest in keeping the tariff in place.
entries.example_spoken: He has a vested interest in the club getting more money.

entries.definition: to be the opposite of something or to conflict with it
entries.example_academic: These results run counter to the predictions of the standard model.
entries.example_spoken: That idea runs counter to everything our professor said.

entries.definition: to make an idea or theory seem more likely to be true
entries.example_academic: The discovery lends support to the theory that the island was settled from the east.
entries.example_spoken: Your story lends support to what I was saying.

entries.definition: a statement about a whole group that is too broad and ignores important differences
entries.example_academic: The article relies on sweeping generalizations about an entire generation.
entries.example_spoken: That's a sweeping generalization; not all engineers hate writing.

entries.definition: to make something seem less certain or less likely to be true
entries.example_academic: Errors in the sampling cast doubt on the study's conclusions.
entries.example_spoken: The missing pages cast doubt on his whole story.

entries.definition: to remain correct or valid in a particular situation
entries.example_academic: The rule holds true for most mammals but not for bats.
entries.example_spoken: Does that still hold true if you study part-time?

entries.definition: to provide something that was missing
entries.example_academic: The study fills a gap in our knowledge of rural diets.
entries.example_spoken: This workshop fills a gap for students who never learned to cite.

entries.definition: the largest part of something
entries.example_academic: The bulk of the funding came from private donors.
entries.example_spoken: I spent the bulk of the weekend in the library.

entries.definition: the most basic reason why a problem exists
entries.example_academic: The report identifies poor drainage as the root cause of the flooding.
entries.example_spoken: The root cause of our delays is that nobody answers emails.

entries.definition: easy to get or obtain
entries.example_academic: Coal was readily available and cheaper than imported oil.
entries.example_spoken: The slides are readily available on the course page.

entries.definition: a connection in which one thing makes another happen
entries.example_academic: A correlation between two variables does not prove a causal relationship.
entries.example_spoken: There might be a link, but is it a causal relationship?

entries.definition: a very clear and noticeable difference
entries.example_academic: The wealth of the capital stood in stark contrast to the poverty of the provinces.
entries.example_spoken: Her calm was in stark contrast to everyone else's panic.

entries.definition: the view that most people accept as true without questioning it
entries.example_academic: The study challenges the conventional wisdom that breakfast improves concentration.
entries.example_spoken: Conventional wisdom says you shouldn't change your first answer.

entries.definition: results of an action that were not planned or expected
entries.example_academic: Price controls often have unintended consequences, such as shortages.
entries.example_spoken: Banning laptops in class had some unintended consequences.

entries.definition: connected so closely that the two things cannot be separated
entries.example_academic: Language and identity are inextricably linked in the history of the region.
entries.example_spoken: For me, coffee and studying are inextricably linked.

entries.definition: to make an idea seem more believable, or to accept it as possibly true
entries.example_academic: The newly discovered letters give credence to the claim that the treaty was forged.
entries.example_spoken: I wouldn't give credence to rumors about the exam.

entries.definition: a question that is no longer worth discussing because it cannot be settled or no longer matters
entries.example_academic: Whether the bridge could have been saved is now a moot point.
entries.example_spoken: It's a moot point now; the class is already full.

entries.definition: to make people want to ask an obvious question; in logic, to assume what you are trying to prove
entries.translation_fr: soulever la question ; faire une pétition de principe
entries.example_academic: The proposal begs the question of who will pay for the maintenance.
entries.example_spoken: That begs the question: why didn't anyone tell us earlier?

entries.definition: a result that is certain before it happens
entries.example_academic: With the opposition divided, the outcome of the vote was a foregone conclusion.
entries.example_spoken: Her winning the prize was a foregone conclusion.

entries.definition: to be suitable for a particular use or treatment
entries.example_academic: The material lends itself to large-scale industrial production.
entries.example_spoken: This topic lends itself to a group presentation.

entries.definition: the most important and difficult part of a problem or argument
entries.example_academic: The crux of the matter is whether the two samples are truly comparable.
entries.example_spoken: The crux of the matter is that we started too late.

entries.definition: full of problems
entries.example_academic: Any attempt to date the manuscript precisely is fraught with difficulty.
entries.example_spoken: Organizing a trip for forty people is fraught with difficulty.

entries.definition: a clear and noticeable change from what was done or expected before
entries.example_academic: The policy represented a marked departure from decades of protectionism.
entries.example_spoken: Her second essay was a marked departure from her usual style.

entries.definition: an understanding that is accepted by everyone without being put into words
entries.example_academic: There was a tacit agreement among producers not to lower prices.
entries.example_spoken: We have a tacit agreement that whoever cooks doesn't wash up.

entries.definition: to make people notice something, especially a problem
entries.example_academic: The report draws attention to the poor condition of rural schools.
entries.example_spoken: I don't want to draw attention to myself in class.
entries.example_interview: In my presentation, I wanted to draw attention to how hard it is to find student housing.
entries.example_discussion: Lena draws attention to a real gap: rural students are absent from the data.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Draw attention to", not "attract the attention on", a common French calque. Irregular: drew, drawn.

entries.definition: to have great power or influence over a group or a field
entries.example_academic: For decades, this interpretation held sway among economic historians.
entries.example_spoken: That idea still holds sway in our department.
entries.example_interview: In my family, my grandmother's opinion still holds sway over every big decision.
entries.example_discussion: This view held sway for decades, but recent research has challenged it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Hold sway over/among". Irregular: held.

entries.definition: to be examined carefully and critically, especially by the public or experts
entries.example_academic: The agency's methods have come under scrutiny after several errors were reported.
entries.example_spoken: The new parking rules are coming under scrutiny from students.
entries.example_interview: My spending came under scrutiny when my parents saw my first bank statement.
entries.example_discussion: Admissions policies have come under scrutiny after several complaints.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "come under fire" (be criticized). Not "be put under scrutiny" in this collocation.

entries.definition: to suffer the worst part of something unpleasant
entries.translation_fr: subir de plein fouet, faire les frais de
entries.example_academic: Low-income households bear the brunt of rising energy prices.
entries.example_spoken: First-year students always bear the brunt of the housing shortage.
entries.example_interview: As the youngest, I usually bore the brunt of my brothers' jokes.
entries.example_discussion: Kim is right that small shops would bear the brunt of the new parking fees.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means suffer the worst part. Irregular: bore, borne.

entries.definition: to give arguments that support an idea or a course of action
entries.example_academic: The author makes a case for treating water as a public good.
entries.example_spoken: You could make a case for moving the exam to next week.
entries.example_interview: I made a case for a later start time, and my manager agreed.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel makes a strong case for public funding, but he ignores the costs.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Make a (strong/compelling) case for". Not "do a case for".

entries.definition: to state that something belongs to you or that you deserve it
entries.example_academic: Several cities lay claim to being the birthplace of the style.
entries.example_spoken: Two people lay claim to the same desk every morning.
entries.example_interview: My little sister lays claim to the front seat every single time.
entries.example_discussion: No single country can lay claim to inventing this idea, so Daniel's framing is misleading.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Lay claim to + noun or -ing". Irregular: laid.

entries.definition: to say that you support something without doing anything to help it
entries.translation_fr: ne soutenir que du bout des lèvres
entries.example_academic: Many firms pay lip service to diversity while changing very little.
entries.example_spoken: They pay lip service to student feedback but never act on it.
entries.example_interview: Some companies pay lip service to work-life balance, but mine really respects it.
entries.example_discussion: Many schools pay lip service to student wellbeing; Mia's proposal would actually fund it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, critical. Means support in words only.

entries.definition: to be obvious or logical
entries.example_academic: It stands to reason that larger samples give more stable estimates.
entries.example_spoken: It stands to reason you'll be tired if you only slept three hours.
entries.example_interview: It stands to reason that I'd want to live close to campus.
entries.example_discussion: It stands to reason that students who work twenty hours a week will study less, as Jonah says.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Almost always "it stands to reason that…". Irregular: stood.

entries.definition: to do something even though it may lead to an unwanted result
entries.example_academic: Studies that rely on self-reports run the risk of underestimating the effect.
entries.example_spoken: If you leave it till Sunday, you run the risk of missing the deadline.
entries.example_interview: If I don't book now, I run the risk of missing the concert.
entries.example_discussion: Schools that rely on a single test run the risk of misjudging students.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Run the risk of + -ing". Not "take the risk to", which means deliberately accept a risk.

entries.definition: to show clearly that something exists or is true
entries.example_academic: The ruins bear witness to a once prosperous trading city.
entries.example_spoken: The empty pizza boxes bear witness to a long night of studying.
entries.example_interview: The photos on my wall bear witness to some great trips.
entries.example_discussion: The empty classrooms Lena describes bear witness to how poorly the reform was planned.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means show or prove. Close to "attest to".

entries.definition: to cause people to criticize something
entries.example_academic: The decision to close the museum on weekends drew sharp criticism.
entries.example_spoken: His comments are drawing a lot of criticism online.
entries.example_interview: My first design drew a lot of criticism, which actually helped me improve it.
entries.example_discussion: The decision drew sharp criticism from parents and teachers.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "draw fire". Not "make criticism", a French calque.

entries.definition: to cause people to worry about something, or to mention worries formally
entries.translation_fr: susciter des inquiétudes, soulever des préoccupations
entries.example_academic: The findings raise concerns about the long-term safety of the additive.
entries.example_spoken: A few students raised concerns about the noise in the library.
entries.example_interview: I raised concerns about the deadline, and the team agreed to move it.
entries.example_discussion: Kim raises concerns about privacy that the professor's question does not address.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Two meanings: cause worry, or formally mention worries. Not "rise concerns" (rise is intransitive).

entries.definition: to create a difficulty that needs to be dealt with
entries.translation_fr: poser un défi, représenter une difficulté
entries.example_academic: Aging populations pose a challenge for public pension systems.
entries.example_spoken: Getting everyone in one room poses a real challenge.
entries.example_interview: Living on my own posed a challenge at first, especially cooking.
entries.example_discussion: Rising rents pose a challenge for universities that want to attract students from poorer families.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "pose a threat/risk/problem". Not "put a challenge".

entries.definition: to be opposed by people when you try to do something
entries.example_academic: The proposal met with resistance from local farmers.
entries.example_spoken: My plan to repaint the kitchen is meeting with resistance from my roommates.
entries.example_interview: When I suggested a four-day week at my old job, it met with resistance from the managers.
entries.example_discussion: Any reform of exams will meet with resistance unless teachers help design it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Irregular: met. Also "meet with approval/success".

entries.definition: to become more popular, accepted or successful
entries.example_academic: The idea gained traction after several cities adopted it successfully.
entries.example_spoken: The petition is finally gaining traction on campus.
entries.example_interview: My idea for a study group gained traction once a few friends joined.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel's idea of shared bikes has gained traction in other cities, which suggests it could work here.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means become accepted or popular. Not "take traction".

entries.definition: to forget an important aim or fact because you are concentrating on something else
entries.example_academic: Reformers sometimes lose sight of the people the policy is meant to serve.
entries.example_spoken: Don't lose sight of why you started this degree.
entries.example_interview: During exams, I try not to lose sight of why I chose this field.
entries.example_discussion: By focusing only on cost, Jonah may lose sight of what students actually need.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Irregular: lost. "Lose sight of + noun".

entries.definition: to be more important than something else and be dealt with first
entries.translation_fr: primer sur, avoir la priorité sur
entries.example_academic: In emergencies, patient safety takes precedence over cost.
entries.example_spoken: Exams take precedence over my part-time job this month.
entries.example_interview: For me, family always takes precedence over work.
entries.example_discussion: Safety must take precedence over cost in any transport project.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Pronounced /ˈprɛsɪdəns/. Not "take the precedence on".

entries.definition: to accept a difficult situation and learn to deal with it
entries.example_academic: Societies often take generations to come to terms with past conflicts.
entries.example_spoken: I'm still coming to terms with my grade on the midterm.
entries.example_interview: It took me a while to come to terms with failing my driving test.
entries.example_discussion: Older workers need time to come to terms with new technology, so training should be gradual.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means accept something painful. Not "come to an agreement" in this sense.

entries.definition: to remain convincing when examined carefully
entries.example_academic: The claim does not stand up to scrutiny once the full data set is considered.
entries.example_spoken: His excuse doesn't really stand up to scrutiny.
entries.example_interview: In my last job, I learned to check my reports twice so they would stand up to scrutiny.
entries.example_discussion: Mia's claim that grades rose does not stand up to scrutiny, since the test itself changed.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "stand up to criticism". Irregular: stood.

entries.definition: to use knowledge, experience or sources to help you do something
entries.example_academic: The novel draws on the author's years as a nurse.
entries.example_spoken: For the presentation, I'm drawing on my internship experience.
entries.example_interview: In interviews, I draw on my experience as a camp counselor.
entries.example_discussion: My argument draws on Kim's example but reaches a different conclusion.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Draw on + experience/sources/knowledge". Not "draw from" in every case, though that also exists.

entries.definition: by a large difference in amount or degree
entries.example_academic: The new design outperformed the older models by a wide margin.
entries.example_spoken: She won the election by a wide margin.
entries.example_interview: My hometown team lost by a wide margin, unfortunately.
entries.example_discussion: The second option is cheaper by a wide margin.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "by a narrow margin". Not "with a wide margin".

entries.definition: in a smaller way or to a smaller degree than the thing just mentioned
entries.example_academic: The reform affected farmers and, to a lesser extent, small traders.
entries.example_spoken: I like coffee and, to a lesser extent, tea.
entries.example_interview: I speak Spanish and, to a lesser extent, Portuguese.
entries.example_discussion: The policy would help families with young children and, to a lesser extent, retired people.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Used after mentioning the main case. Not "in a lesser extent".

entries.definition: a typical example of something that has just been described
entries.example_academic: Many towns grew around a single industry; the mill village studied here is a case in point.
entries.example_spoken: Group projects can be chaotic. Last week's presentation is a case in point.
entries.example_interview: I learn best by doing; my summer job in a lab is a case in point.
entries.example_discussion: Many towns depend on one industry, and the mining region is a case in point.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Usually "X is a case in point". Introduces a typical example of what was just said.

entries.definition: a subject about which people disagree
entries.example_academic: The date of the manuscript remains a point of contention among scholars.
entries.example_spoken: Who does the dishes is a constant point of contention in our flat.
entries.example_interview: At my last job, the holiday schedule was a point of contention, and I helped find a compromise.
entries.example_discussion: The cost of the program remains the main point of contention.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "bone of contention" (informal).

entries.definition: a problem that stops an agreement or a process from moving forward
entries.example_academic: Funding for maintenance was the main sticking point in the negotiations.
entries.example_spoken: The price is the only sticking point for me.
entries.example_interview: When I chose my university, the cost of housing was the main sticking point.
entries.example_discussion: The main sticking point in Daniel's plan is who would pay for the extra buses.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means an obstacle to agreement.

entries.definition: a situation in which the rules or the right answer are not clear
entries.example_academic: The use of public photographs for training models remains a legal grey area.
entries.example_spoken: Whether you can bring food into the library is a bit of a grey area.
entries.example_interview: When I worked in a shop, returns without a receipt were a grey area, so I always asked my manager.
entries.example_discussion: Whether teachers may use students' work in research is a grey area that the policy should clarify.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Spelled "gray area" in American English. Both spellings are accepted.

entries.definition: a situation in which one problem causes another that then makes the first worse
entries.example_academic: Poverty and poor health can form a vicious circle across generations.
entries.example_spoken: Not sleeping makes me stressed, and stress keeps me awake: a vicious circle.
entries.example_interview: In my first year I got into a vicious circle: I was behind, so I skipped class, so I fell further behind.
entries.example_discussion: Cutting bus routes because few people ride them can create a vicious circle, as Jonah's example shows.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Vicious cycle" is also used, especially in American English.

entries.definition: a rule that is applied unfairly to one group but not to another
entries.example_academic: The study exposes a double standard in how male and female candidates are judged.
entries.example_spoken: It's a double standard to let him miss class but not me.
entries.example_interview: It felt like a double standard that my brother could stay out later than me.
entries.example_discussion: Judging male and female candidates differently is a clear double standard.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Usually singular: "a double standard". Not "a double weight".

entries.definition: the opinion generally accepted by experts at a particular time
entries.example_academic: The received view held that the empire collapsed suddenly, but new evidence suggests a slow decline.
entries.example_spoken: The received view in our class is that the final is easy.
entries.example_interview: The received view in my family was that medicine was the best career.
entries.example_discussion: Kim challenges the received view that private schools always perform better.
entries.usage_note: Formal, academic. Also "received wisdom". Means the generally accepted opinion.

entries.definition: the most important worry or consideration, more important than all others
entries.example_academic: Safety must remain the overriding concern in the design of the bridge.
entries.example_spoken: My overriding concern right now is finding an apartment.
entries.example_interview: My overriding concern when choosing a flat was safety.
entries.example_discussion: For most parents, cost is not the overriding concern; safety is.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Overriding" = more important than everything else.

entries.definition: changes that affect many parts of a system at once
entries.example_academic: The new government introduced sweeping reforms to the tax system.
entries.example_spoken: They're talking about sweeping reforms to the meal plan.
entries.example_interview: My school went through sweeping reforms just after I left.
entries.example_discussion: Sweeping reforms rarely succeed without the support of teachers.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Sweeping" = wide-ranging. Also "sweeping changes".

entries.definition: a rise that is large enough to be clearly noticed
entries.example_academic: The data show a marked increase in cycling after the new lanes opened.
entries.example_spoken: There's been a marked increase in the price of coffee here.
entries.example_interview: Since I started cycling to class, I've noticed a marked increase in my energy levels.
entries.example_discussion: The data show a marked increase in remote work since 2020.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Marked" = clearly noticeable. Pronounced /mɑːrkt/, one syllable.

entries.definition: a gradual and continuous fall
entries.example_academic: The town experienced a steady decline in population after the mine closed.
entries.example_spoken: There's been a steady decline in attendance since October.
entries.example_interview: My grandparents' village has seen a steady decline in population.
entries.example_discussion: Newspapers have experienced a steady decline in readership.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Opposite: "steady increase/growth".

entries.definition: a difficult problem that people have argued about for a long time
entries.example_academic: The vexed question of who owns the river's water has never been settled.
entries.example_spoken: Where to go for spring break is a vexed question in our group.
entries.example_interview: Where to spend the holidays is a vexed question in my family.
entries.example_discussion: How to fund rural schools remains a vexed question, and neither post fully answers it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means a difficult, much-debated problem.

entries.definition: a task that is very difficult and needs a lot of effort over time
entries.example_academic: Persuading voters to accept higher taxes is an uphill struggle.
entries.example_spoken: Learning statistics has been an uphill struggle for me.
entries.example_interview: Getting my first internship was an uphill struggle, because I had no contacts in the industry.
entries.example_discussion: Mia underestimates what an uphill struggle it is to recruit teachers for rural schools.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "uphill battle".

entries.definition: a rule that forbids something completely, with no exceptions
entries.example_academic: The council rejected a blanket ban on short-term rentals.
entries.example_spoken: A blanket ban on phones in class seems a bit extreme.
entries.example_interview: My old school had a blanket ban on phones, which I thought was too strict.
entries.example_discussion: A blanket ban on cars downtown would penalize people with disabilities.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Blanket" = applying to everything without exceptions.

entries.definition: a very obvious and important thing that has been left out
entries.example_academic: The absence of women's testimony is a glaring omission in the official history.
entries.example_spoken: Forgetting the deadline in the email was a glaring omission.
entries.example_interview: Looking back, a glaring omission in my first CV was my volunteer work.
entries.example_discussion: The absence of teachers from the survey is a glaring omission.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Glaring" = very obvious, in a negative sense.

entries.definition: a very small difference that separates two things
entries.example_academic: There is a fine line between simplifying a theory and distorting it.
entries.example_spoken: There's a fine line between confident and arrogant.
entries.example_interview: In interviews, I try to walk the fine line between confident and boastful.
entries.example_discussion: There is a fine line between encouraging healthy habits and controlling students' lives, and Daniel's plan crosses it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "A fine line between X and Y". Also "a thin line".

entries.definition: the responsibility for showing that a claim is true
entries.example_academic: The burden of proof lies with those who claim the treatment is effective.
entries.example_spoken: If you say I broke it, the burden of proof is on you.
entries.example_interview: My friend claimed I broke his phone, so the burden of proof was on him.
entries.example_discussion: If Daniel claims the scheme saves money, the burden of proof is on him to show the figures.
entries.usage_note: Formal, legal origin. "The burden of proof lies with / is on…".

entries.definition: the stage after which it is no longer possible to stop or go back
entries.example_academic: Once the funds were transferred, the project had passed the point of no return.
entries.example_spoken: I've paid the deposit, so I'm past the point of no return.
entries.example_interview: Once I had signed the lease abroad, I knew I was past the point of no return.
entries.example_discussion: Some scientists fear the ice sheet is near the point of no return.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often "past/beyond the point of no return".

entries.definition: an indirect result of an action that affects other things in turn
entries.example_academic: The factory closure had a knock-on effect on local shops and schools.
entries.example_spoken: The bus strike had a knock-on effect on everyone's morning.
entries.example_interview: Losing my part-time job had a knock-on effect on my studies, because I had to find another one fast.
entries.example_discussion: Higher tuition fees could have a knock-on effect on rural towns, as fewer young people return.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, more British. American English often prefers "ripple effect".

entries.definition: very noticeable because something expected is missing
entries.example_academic: Any discussion of cost is conspicuous by its absence in the final report.
entries.example_spoken: Any mention of free food was conspicuous by its absence in the email.
entries.example_interview: When we planned the move, any offer of help from my brother was conspicuous by its absence.
entries.example_discussion: In Jonah's post, any mention of teachers is conspicuous by its absence.
entries.usage_note: Formal, ironic. The possessive changes with the subject: "by his/her/its absence".

entries.definition: a decisive test that shows whether something is really good or true
entries.example_academic: The acid test of the theory will be whether it predicts next year's results.
entries.example_spoken: The real acid test is whether the new app works during exams.
entries.example_interview: The real acid test for my new schedule will be exam week.
entries.example_discussion: The acid test for Kim's proposal is whether students actually use the new space.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means a decisive test. Also "litmus test".

entries.definition: to be the opposite of what is generally accepted or expected
entries.example_academic: These results fly in the face of everything we thought we knew about the species.
entries.example_spoken: Skipping breakfast flies in the face of all the advice I've been given.
entries.example_interview: Skipping breakfast flies in the face of everything my mother taught me.
entries.example_discussion: These results fly in the face of conventional wisdom about diet.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means contradict something accepted. Irregular: flew.

entries.definition: to be closely connected and happen together
entries.example_academic: In many regions, economic growth goes hand in hand with rising inequality.
entries.example_spoken: Good grades usually go hand in hand with good sleep.
entries.example_interview: For me, creativity goes hand in hand with a bit of chaos.
entries.example_discussion: Better pay should go hand in hand with better training, as Mia argues.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means occur together. Not "go hand by hand".

entries.definition: not certain, and possible to doubt or challenge
entries.example_academic: Whether the effect applies to adults remains open to question.
entries.example_spoken: His version of the story is open to question.
entries.example_interview: Whether that was the right choice is still open to question.
entries.example_discussion: Whether online classes are as effective as in-person ones is still open to question.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means uncertain or debatable.

entries.definition: despite having to deal with a difficult situation or opposition
entries.example_academic: The project continued in the face of strong local opposition.
entries.example_spoken: She stayed calm in the face of some pretty rude questions.
entries.example_interview: My parents stayed calm in the face of some serious difficulties.
entries.example_discussion: Small farms have survived in the face of strong competition, which supports Lena's point.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means despite or when confronted with.

entries.headword: err on the side of caution
entries.definition: to choose the safer option when you are not sure what to do
entries.example_academic: When the data are uncertain, regulators tend to err on the side of caution.
entries.example_spoken: I'd err on the side of caution and bring an umbrella.
entries.example_interview: I always err on the side of caution and arrive early for interviews.
entries.example_discussion: With children's data, schools should err on the side of caution, as Daniel suggests.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Pronounced /ɜːr/, like "her". Not "make an error on the side".

entries.definition: in effect, though not officially or exactly
entries.example_academic: By 1920, the old guild system had, to all intents and purposes, disappeared.
entries.example_spoken: To all intents and purposes, the project is finished.
entries.example_interview: To all intents and purposes, my brother runs the family business now.
entries.example_discussion: If the fee is that high, the course is, to all intents and purposes, closed to poorer students.
entries.usage_note: Formal. American English also uses "for all intents and purposes". Never "to all intensive purposes".

entries.definition: not in agreement or not consistent with something
entries.translation_fr: en contradiction avec, en désaccord avec
entries.example_academic: The official figures are at odds with the accounts of local residents.
entries.example_spoken: My plans are totally at odds with my budget.
entries.example_interview: A job with no free weekends would be at odds with my priorities right now.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel's proposal is at odds with the goal he himself sets out in his first sentence.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means in disagreement or inconsistent with.

entries.definition: a reason or set of reasons so strong that it is difficult to disagree
entries.example_academic: The authors make a compelling argument for regulating the industry.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pretty compelling argument for leaving early.
entries.example_interview: My manager made a compelling argument for staying, so I postponed my move.
entries.example_discussion: Lena makes a compelling argument, but she relies on a single example.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Make a compelling argument/case for". French speakers often say "a convincing argument", which is fine but weaker.

entries.definition: to explain or show that two similar things are different
entries.example_academic: The author draws a clear distinction between equality and equity.
entries.example_spoken: You have to draw a distinction between being tired and being lazy.
entries.example_interview: I always draw a distinction between friends and colleagues, even when I like my colleagues.
entries.example_discussion: We need to draw a distinction between short-term costs and long-term benefits.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Draw a distinction between X and Y". "Make a distinction" is also correct. Not "do a distinction". Irregular: drew, drawn.

entries.definition: a connection that is very weak or hard to prove
entries.example_academic: The report suggests only a tenuous link between diet and the disease.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pretty tenuous link, if you ask me.
entries.example_interview: There's only a tenuous link between my degree and my first job, but the skills transferred.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah draws only a tenuous link between phones and grades, since other factors are ignored.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "tenuous connection/evidence". French "ténu" exists but is rarely translated this way by learners.

entries.definition: an idea used as the starting point of an argument that is wrong or weak
entries.example_academic: The model rests on a flawed premise about how consumers behave.
entries.example_spoken: The whole plan starts from a flawed premise.
entries.example_interview: My first business idea was built on a flawed premise: I assumed students had money to spend.
entries.example_discussion: The proposal rests on a flawed premise, namely that all families own a computer.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Premise" is pronounced /ˈprɛmɪs/. Also "a false premise".

entries.definition: a discussion in which people disagree angrily and bitterly
entries.example_academic: The reform followed an acrimonious debate in parliament.
entries.example_spoken: We had a pretty acrimonious debate about chores.
entries.example_interview: There was an acrimonious debate in my family about where to spend the holidays.
entries.example_discussion: An acrimonious debate rarely changes minds, which is why Mia's compromise matters.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Stronger than "heated debate". Also "acrimonious divorce/dispute".

entries.definition: a majority that is very small
entries.example_academic: The measure passed by a slender majority of three votes.
entries.example_spoken: They only won by a slender majority.
entries.example_interview: Our student council elected me by a slender majority, so I felt I had to listen to everyone.
entries.example_discussion: A policy adopted by a slender majority needs broad consultation to last.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Narrow majority" is more common; "slender" sounds more precise and written.

entries.definition: a sudden increase in public support for something
entries.example_academic: The campaign benefited from a groundswell of support among young voters.
entries.example_spoken: There's been a real groundswell of support for the new park.
entries.example_interview: Our petition for longer library hours got a groundswell of support in just a week.
entries.example_discussion: Without a groundswell of support from parents, the reform is unlikely to succeed.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "groundswell of opinion/opposition".

entries.definition: to make people feel less worried about something
entries.example_academic: The minister tried to allay fears about the safety of the vaccine.
entries.example_spoken: I called my parents to allay their fears.
entries.example_interview: I sent my parents daily photos during my first month abroad to allay their fears.
entries.example_discussion: Clear information would allay fears about the new transport plan.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "allay concerns/doubts". Not "ally", a different word.

entries.definition: to keep doubts in your mind for a long time
entries.example_academic: Many economists harbor doubts about the forecast.
entries.example_spoken: I still harbor doubts about his plan.
entries.example_interview: I harbored doubts about studying abroad, but they disappeared after the first week.
entries.example_discussion: Many teachers harbor doubts about the new curriculum, as Kim points out.
entries.usage_note: Formal. British spelling "harbour". Also "harbor a grudge/suspicion".

entries.definition: to make people more afraid or worried
entries.example_academic: Rumors of job cuts stoked fears among the staff.
entries.example_spoken: Those headlines just stoke fears.
entries.example_interview: Some news channels stoke fears about cities, but I've always felt safe here.
entries.example_discussion: Exaggerated statistics only stoke fears instead of informing the debate.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Opposite of "allay fears". Also "stoke tensions/anger".

entries.definition: to cause people to make more guesses about something
entries.example_academic: His sudden resignation fueled speculation about a merger.
entries.example_spoken: Her silence just fueled speculation.
entries.example_interview: My long absence from social media fueled speculation among my friends that I'd moved.
entries.example_discussion: Delaying the report will only fuel speculation that the results are bad.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. British spelling "fuelled". Also "fuel concerns/debate".

entries.definition: a very obvious and serious violation of a rule or law
entries.example_academic: The decision was a flagrant breach of international law.
entries.example_spoken: That's a flagrant breach of the rules.
entries.example_interview: Copying a classmate's work would be a flagrant breach of trust, and I'd never do it.
entries.example_discussion: Sharing students' data without consent would be a flagrant breach of privacy.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Flagrant" is transparent; the collocation with "breach" is the useful part. Not "flagrant violation of a promise".

entries.definition: a small action done to show support, but not enough to make a real difference
entries.example_academic: The small grant was seen as a token gesture by local farmers.
entries.example_spoken: Planting one tree is just a token gesture.
entries.example_interview: Our company's green week felt like a token gesture, so I suggested real changes.
entries.example_discussion: A single meat-free day would be a token gesture unless it changes long-term habits.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, critical. "Token" = symbolic, insufficient. Different from "goodwill gesture" (positive).

entries.definition: a claim that someone did something wrong, with no evidence to support it
entries.example_academic: The minister dismissed the report as an unfounded allegation.
entries.example_spoken: That's an unfounded allegation, and you know it.
entries.example_interview: When someone made an unfounded allegation against my team, we answered with facts.
entries.example_discussion: Calling the study biased is an unfounded allegation unless Daniel shows evidence.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "unfounded claim/fears". "Allegation" has four syllables.

entries.definition: a conflict that is a natural part of a situation and cannot be avoided
entries.example_academic: There is an inherent tension between privacy and security.
entries.example_spoken: There's an inherent tension in being a student and an employee.
entries.example_interview: There's an inherent tension between studying full time and working, and I manage it with strict planning.
entries.example_discussion: Mia's plan contains an inherent tension between giving schools freedom and holding them accountable.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "An inherent tension between X and Y".

entries.definition: to set a higher standard that others must reach
entries.example_academic: The new regulations raise the bar for safety in the industry.
entries.example_spoken: Her performance has really raised the bar.
entries.example_interview: My last internship raised the bar for what I expect from an employer.
entries.example_discussion: Stricter rules would raise the bar for every school, not only the weakest ones.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, idiomatic. Same image as "placer la barre plus haut". Opposite: "lower the bar".

entries.definition: to do something that can be used later as an example or justification
entries.example_academic: The ruling set a precedent for similar cases.
entries.example_spoken: If we let him skip, it sets a precedent.
entries.example_interview: When I asked for flexible hours, my manager worried it would set a precedent.
entries.example_discussion: Exempting one school would set a precedent that others would soon follow.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Precedent" is stressed on the first syllable. Not "make a precedent".

entries.definition: to express disagreement formally or openly
entries.example_academic: Several members voiced an objection to the new rules.
entries.example_spoken: I voiced my objection, but nobody listened.
entries.example_interview: In meetings, I try to voice an objection politely rather than staying silent.
entries.example_discussion: I would like to voice an objection to the idea that tests measure intelligence.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "voice concerns/support". Not "say an objection".

entries.definition: to consider all the facts carefully before deciding
entries.example_academic: Jurors must weigh the evidence before reaching a verdict.
entries.example_spoken: Let's weigh the evidence before we decide.
entries.example_interview: Before changing majors, I weighed the evidence carefully, including job prospects.
entries.example_discussion: If we weigh the evidence fairly, the second option seems more realistic.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Evidence" is uncountable: never "evidences".

entries.definition: to come to a final decision after careful consideration, especially in a court
entries.translation_fr: rendre un verdict, parvenir à un verdict
entries.example_academic: The jury reached a verdict after three days.
entries.example_spoken: Have you reached a verdict on the new phone?
entries.example_interview: After testing both laptops for a week, I reached a verdict: lighter is better.
entries.example_discussion: It is too early to reach a verdict on the policy after only one year.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also figurative. Not "give a verdict" for juries in English (judges deliver the sentence).

entries.definition: to have to pay costs as a result of an action
entries.translation_fr: engager des frais, supporter des coûts
entries.example_academic: Firms that delay compliance may incur substantial costs.
entries.example_spoken: You'll incur extra costs if you cancel late.
entries.example_interview: I incurred some unexpected costs when I moved, so I took a weekend job.
entries.example_discussion: Cities that delay maintenance incur far higher costs later.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "incur debt/a penalty/losses". Past: "incurred", double r.

entries.definition: to produce results, especially after effort or time
entries.translation_fr: donner des résultats, porter ses fruits
entries.example_academic: The new treatment has yet to yield results in larger trials.
entries.example_spoken: All that practice is finally yielding results.
entries.example_interview: My new study routine started to yield results after a month.
entries.example_discussion: Short campaigns rarely yield lasting results without follow-up.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "yield benefits/insights". Not "give results" in formal writing.

entries.definition: to use influence to try to make someone do something
entries.example_academic: Lobby groups exert pressure on lawmakers throughout the year.
entries.example_spoken: My parents never exerted pressure on me to study medicine.
entries.example_interview: My coach exerted a lot of pressure on us, but it made us better.
entries.example_discussion: Parents can exert pressure on schools, which is not always a bad thing.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Exert pressure on someone". "Put pressure on" is the neutral equivalent.

entries.definition: to limit or reduce the amount of gas or pollution released
entries.translation_fr: réduire les émissions, limiter les émissions
entries.example_academic: The treaty aims to curb emissions from shipping.
entries.example_spoken: They want to curb emissions without hurting jobs.
entries.example_interview: I cycle to work partly to curb my own emissions, though it's a small step.
entries.example_discussion: Taxes alone will not curb emissions unless clean alternatives are affordable.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Curb" = restrain. Also "curb spending/inflation".

entries.definition: to cause a strong negative reaction from many people
entries.example_academic: The fee increase sparked a backlash among students.
entries.example_spoken: That ad sparked a huge backlash online.
entries.example_interview: When my school changed the uniform rules, it sparked a backlash among students.
entries.example_discussion: A sudden ban could spark a backlash that undermines the whole policy.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "provoke a backlash". "Backlash against something".

entries.definition: to question whether a belief that people take for granted is true
entries.translation_fr: remettre en cause une hypothèse, un présupposé
entries.example_academic: The study challenges the assumption that older workers adapt slowly.
entries.example_spoken: I like teachers who challenge my assumptions.
entries.example_interview: Living abroad challenged my assumption that my way of doing things was normal.
entries.example_discussion: Mia challenges the assumption that competition always improves quality.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. French speakers sometimes use "challenge" to mean "défi" only; here it means question.

entries.definition: a very clear and serious warning about danger
entries.translation_fr: avertissement sévère, mise en garde sans détour
entries.example_academic: The report issued a stark warning about rising sea levels.
entries.example_spoken: The doctor gave me a stark warning about my diet.
entries.example_interview: My first exam result was a stark warning that I needed to change my habits.
entries.example_discussion: The figures are a stark warning to cities that still rely on cars.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Stark" = harsh and plain. Also "stark contrast/choice".

entries.definition: to agree to something you did not want, in order to reach an agreement
entries.example_academic: The union made a concession on working hours.
entries.example_spoken: I made a concession and let him pick the restaurant.
entries.example_interview: In group projects, I'm willing to make a concession if it keeps the team together.
entries.example_discussion: Both sides would need to make a concession for the plan to work.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Make concessions to someone". Not "do a concession". Irregular: made.

entries.definition: competition that is extremely fierce and ruthless
entries.example_academic: Cut-throat competition has driven many small airlines out of business.
entries.example_spoken: There's cut-throat competition for internships in this city.
entries.example_interview: There's cut-throat competition for places in my program, so I had to stand out.
entries.example_discussion: Cut-throat competition between schools may push them to focus only on test scores.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Also spelled "cutthroat". Stronger than "fierce competition".

entries.definition: to reject an idea immediately, without considering it seriously
entries.example_academic: The committee dismissed the proposal out of hand.
entries.example_spoken: Don't dismiss the idea out of hand.
entries.example_interview: I used to dismiss online courses out of hand, but now I take one every summer.
entries.example_discussion: We should not dismiss Kim's suggestion out of hand just because it is unusual.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. The object goes between the verb and "out of hand". Not "out of the hand".

entries.definition: a general increase over a period of time
entries.example_academic: Rainfall data show a clear upward trend since 1980.
entries.example_spoken: There's been an upward trend in bike use.
entries.example_interview: I've noticed an upward trend in my scores since I started reviewing every evening.
entries.example_discussion: There is an upward trend in remote work, which supports Kim's plan for flexible hours.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Opposite: "downward trend". "Trend" alone does not say up or down.

entries.definition: a very small increase
entries.example_academic: The policy led to only a marginal increase in recycling.
entries.example_spoken: There was a marginal increase in my salary.
entries.example_interview: My new routine gave only a marginal increase in study time, so I changed it again.
entries.example_discussion: A marginal increase in fees would not deter students, in my view.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Marginal" = very small, not "marginal" as in "fringe". Also "marginally higher".

entries.definition: a large and rapid increase
entries.example_academic: The steep rise in food prices hit poor families hardest.
entries.example_spoken: There's been a steep rise in rent.
entries.example_interview: A steep rise in my rent forced me to look for a roommate.
entries.example_discussion: The steep rise in screen time among children is what worries me most.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Steep" comes from slopes on a graph. Also "a steep decline". Not "strong rise".

entries.definition: a sudden and large fall
entries.example_academic: There was a sharp drop in sales after the scandal.
entries.example_spoken: I noticed a sharp drop in my energy at night.
entries.example_interview: After I cut sugar, there was a sharp drop in my afternoon tiredness.
entries.example_discussion: The sharp drop in attendance after the fee rise speaks for itself.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Sharp" = sudden and large. Also "a sharp rise/increase". Not "hard drop".

entries.definition: an increase that makes something twice as large
entries.example_academic: The study found a twofold increase in risk among smokers.
entries.example_spoken: We saw a twofold increase in signups.
entries.example_interview: Our club saw a twofold increase in members after we started posting videos.
entries.example_discussion: A twofold increase in bus frequency would change commuting habits, I believe.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "threefold", "tenfold". As adverb: "increase twofold".

entries.definition: the largest part of something
entries.example_academic: The capital receives the lion's share of public investment.
entries.example_spoken: My brother always took the lion's share of dessert.
entries.example_interview: Rent takes the lion's share of my monthly budget.
entries.example_discussion: Sports already get the lion's share of the activities budget, so arts deserve more.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Always "the lion's share of". Same image as in French.

entries.definition: a very small part or amount of something
entries.translation_fr: une infime partie de, une fraction de
entries.example_academic: Solar power still provides a fraction of total energy.
entries.example_spoken: It costs a fraction of the price.
entries.example_interview: Second-hand books cost a fraction of the price of new ones, so I always buy them.
entries.example_discussion: Online courses cost a fraction of campus fees, which matters for working students.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. In everyday use it means a small part, not an exact proportion as in math. "A fraction of the cost" is very common.
